plain: The held-out loss is the model's error measured on examples it never trained on, so it shows how well the model does on new data and not how well it memorised.
ours: Our head trainer scores a fixed held-out set, so two runs are compared on identical items; for the noise-level split below we use the same crops and the same noise at ten fixed noise levels. Differences below about 0.01 are within run-to-run noise (the same recipe and seed gave 0.1802 and 0.1896). Our best head sits near 0.18.
deeper: Splitting the held-out loss by noise level t shows that about half of it sits at t above 0.7, where the input is nearly pure noise and the optimizer barely matters. That is why optimizer comparisons differ by only a few percent and why the loss curves of different optimizers track each other closely. For LoRA and DoRA the guide advises choosing a checkpoint by listening, not by held-out loss alone.

quiz.q: What is held-out loss measured on?
options: Examples the model never trained on
quiz.why: Held-out data is kept aside so the score shows generalisation.

quiz.q: The same recipe and seed gave 0.1802 and 0.1896. What does that tell you?
options: Differences smaller than about 0.01 may be noise
quiz.why: Repeating a run gives a spread, so smaller differences cannot be trusted.

quiz.q: Why do different optimizers' loss curves track each other closely?
options: About half the loss sits at high noise levels where the optimizer barely matters
They are secretly the same optimizer
All optimizers use the same learning rate
quiz.why: At noise levels near 1 the input is almost pure noise, and most of the loss there does not depend on the optimizer.

plain: The batch size is how many training examples are processed together before the weights are changed once.
ours: Our LoRA and DoRA runs used batches of 1 to 16 and our full fine-tunes 1 to 8 (they are large models). The control heads were trained at effective batches of 8 up to 256; 'effective' means the size after accumulating gradients over several smaller batches. Batch 64 gave our best held-out loss.
deeper: A small batch is a small sample of the data, so its gradient carries a lot of noise; a larger batch gives fewer, less noisy steps over the same data. Compare batch sizes at equal numbers of steps, not equal epochs, or you compare how many steps each had. The noise-limited batch size, called B_simple in the literature, estimates where noise stops being the main problem.

papers.title: An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training (McCandlish et al.)

quiz.q: What is a batch?
options: The group of examples used for one weight change
quiz.why: A batch is the sample used to compute one gradient.

quiz.q: A batch of 4 gives a noisier gradient than a batch of 64 because...
quiz.why: A smaller sample gives a noisier estimate of the true gradient.

quiz.q: In one sweep, batch 32 ran half as many steps as batch 16 in the same number of epochs. What should you do before comparing them?
options: Compare at equal numbers of steps, or say you did not
quiz.why: Otherwise the result mixes the batch-size effect with the step-count effect.

plain: Gradient accumulation adds up the gradients of several small batches and changes the weights once, which gives the effect of a bigger batch without needing the memory for it.
ours: Our heads are compute-bound on the GPU, so an epoch takes the same time at any effective batch. Two traps: in our Stable Audio 3 fine-tuning trainers the EMA of the weights updates on every small batch, not once per weight change, so accumulation shortens the EMA's memory measured in weight changes; and anything that compares consecutive gradients sees only the combined steps.
deeper: For a loss that is a plain sum over examples, accumulation gives the same gradient as one large batch. It differs when the loss or a layer depends on the other examples in the batch (batch-dependent layers, losses that use in-batch negatives), when gradient clipping or normalisation is applied per small batch and not to the sum, and when a per-step statistic is measured.

quiz.q: What does gradient accumulation do?
options: Adds up gradients from several small batches before one weight change
quiz.why: It builds a larger effective batch out of smaller ones.

quiz.q: Is accumulation always identical to a true larger batch?
options: No, not when layers or losses depend on the other examples in the batch
No, because it uses a different optimizer
quiz.why: It matches for plain summed losses and differs for batch-dependent pieces.

quiz.q: Our EMA updates on every small batch. What happens to its memory, measured in weight changes, when you accumulate more?
quiz.why: With more small batches per weight change, the same per-batch decay covers fewer weight changes.

plain: An EMA is a second, slowly updated copy of the weights that follows the training weights with a delay, smoothing out the noise of single steps.
ours: A trainer can save both the live weights and the EMA copy. We once rendered an EMA by default that had barely moved from the starting model, so what we heard was mostly the starting model, not the fine-tune. In our Stable Audio 3 fine-tuning trainers the EMA updates on every small batch, not once per weight change, so accumulation changes how far back it looks.
deeper: An EMA decay of 0.9999 means a half-life of about 6,931 updates. Moving to a different batch size needs a changed decay (the new decay is the old one raised to the ratio of batch sizes) to keep the same time span. A decay that is too long for a short run leaves the EMA close to its starting point. Several tools prefer the EMA copy when a checkpoint carries one, so check which copy your render script loads.

quiz.q: What is an EMA copy of the weights?
options: A slowly updated copy that follows the training weights with a delay
quiz.why: It is a smoothed average of the weights over recent updates.

quiz.q: A run is short, and the EMA decay is far too long for it. What do you hear when rendering with the EMA weights?
quiz.why: A too-long EMA barely moves away from its start in a short run.

quiz.q: An EMA decay of 0.9999 has a half-life of about...
quiz.why: The half-life is ln 0.5 / ln 0.9999, about 6,931 updates.

quiz.q: You switch to a bigger accumulated batch. Why might the EMA decay need changing?
options: The EMA updates per small batch, so its time span in weight changes shifts
The EMA does not depend on batch size
quiz.why: Decay is a timescale in EMA updates, which are counted per small batch.

plain: Warmup starts training with a small learning rate and raises it to full over the first few percent of the run; cosine decay then lowers it smoothly along a half-cosine curve toward zero.
ours: The fine-tuning paper the guide cites uses cosine decay with 3% warmup. The guide's starting configuration uses warmup plus either Schedule-Free averaging or a decaying schedule, and avoids a constant learning rate. The weight-size check starts after warmup.
deeper: Warmup protects the first steps, when the weights and the optimizer's averages are not yet settled. Decay lowers the step size late so the weights settle into a good place. Schedule-Free replaces the decay by averaging the weights.

quiz.q: What does warmup do?
options: Starts with a small learning rate and raises it
Lowers the learning rate at the end
quiz.why: It ramps the learning rate up over the first few percent of the run.

quiz.q: What does cosine decay do?
options: Lowers the learning rate smoothly toward zero
quiz.why: The learning rate follows a half-cosine down.

quiz.q: Which method in this guide replaces a decaying schedule?
quiz.why: Schedule-Free keeps the learning rate and averages the weights.

plain: Gradient clipping caps the overall size of the gradient at a set limit, so one unusually large batch cannot cause a huge step.
ours: Our recent head runs used a clip of 1.0. In one full fine-tune, clipping at 1.0 did not change the pattern of loss spikes: 38% of steps still spiked above 5.
deeper: Clipping rescales the whole gradient when its norm exceeds the limit, leaving its direction alone. It protects against single bad batches but does not fix a systematic problem such as the weights growing, and an optimizer that normalises the size of its update (Muon, sign steps) is already insensitive to the gradient's size.

quiz.q: What does gradient clipping do?
options: Caps the gradient's overall size at a limit
quiz.why: It rescales a too-large gradient down to the limit.

quiz.q: Did clipping at 1.0 fix the loss spikes in our full fine-tune?
options: No, 38% of steps still spiked above 5
quiz.why: The guide reports the spikes continued.

quiz.q: Why is clipping less relevant for an optimizer that normalises its update size?
options: The step size no longer depends on the gradient's size
quiz.why: If the step is already fixed in size, scaling the gradient changes nothing.

plain: NaN means 'not a number': a value that has become undefined, usually from overflow or dividing zero by zero, and once it enters the weights everything computed from them is ruined.
ours: In our runs NaN showed up in a head at epoch 13 (run B3) and in a DoRA run near step 6,900. Our head trainer now stops at the first non-finite loss. A check written as 'if the value is greater than X' cannot detect NaN, because any comparison with NaN is false; one of the optimizers we audited had exactly this bug.
deeper: NaN rarely appears out of nowhere: weights or magnitudes usually grew, or crossed zero, for hundreds of steps before the loss turned NaN. That is why the guide logs weight size and update size per group, and checks that saved weights and test outputs are finite, both.

quiz.q: What does NaN mean?
options: Not a number, an undefined value
quiz.why: It is the result of an undefined operation such as 0 divided by 0.

quiz.q: Why can a check 'loss > limit' miss a NaN loss?
options: Any comparison with NaN is false
quiz.why: NaN is neither greater nor smaller than anything, so such guards never fire.

quiz.q: What usually happens before a run's loss turns NaN?
options: Weights or magnitudes grow or cross zero for a while
quiz.why: The guide's failures all showed earlier warning signs in weight size or magnitudes.

plain: A loss spike is a step whose loss jumps far above the typical value; counting spikes and tracking the median shows trouble that an average hides.
ours: In one full fine-tune the average loss in each logging bin fell from 405 to 84 and looked like convergence, while the median stayed at 2.5 against 0.79 for the reference run, and 38% of steps spiked above 5. Five matters because the reference run's median was 0.79, so 5 is more than six times a normal step.
deeper: A mean is dragged by a few huge values, so it can fall steadily while most steps stay bad. The median shows the typical step, and the share of steps above a threshold shows how often things go wrong. Pick the threshold relative to the reference run's typical loss, not as an absolute number.

quiz.q: What is a loss spike?
options: A step whose loss jumps far above the typical value
The first loss of the run
quiz.why: It is an outlier in the loss.

quiz.q: Why can the mean loss mislead?
options: A few huge values can dominate it and hide that most steps are bad
It is computed on test data
quiz.why: The mean was falling while the median stayed high.

quiz.q: Why is a loss of 5 a lot in the example?
options: The reference run's median was 0.79, so 5 is over six times typical
quiz.why: Spike thresholds make sense relative to the typical loss of a healthy run.

plain: A logging bin is a stretch of consecutive training steps whose losses are summarised into one logged point, so the log is a manageable curve and not one line per step.
ours: The trainer's logging setting decides how long a bin is; the guide's example does not state the bin length. What matters is how the bin is summarised: the average of a bin can fall because of a few extreme steps, so the guide recommends logging the median and a count of spikes per bin as well.
deeper: Larger bins smooth the curve and hide single steps; smaller bins show noise. The 'mean of each logging bin fell from 405 to 84' example is the average of every step in each stretch.

quiz.q: What is a logging bin?
options: A group of consecutive steps summarised in one logged point
quiz.why: It is a stretch of steps reduced to a single value.

quiz.q: Who decides how long a bin is?
quiz.why: It is a trainer option; the guide does not state our bin length.

quiz.q: Why log the median and the spike count per bin in addition to the mean?
options: The mean can fall because of a few extreme steps
quiz.why: The 405-to-84 mean looked like convergence while the median showed nothing had improved.

plain: The path of the weights is the route all the weights take through training; we measure how far they have moved from the start, how fast per step, and how straight the route is.
ours: Path efficiency is the straight-line distance from the start divided by the total length of the route. It did not separate healthy from runaway DoRA runs on its own (runaways read 0.14 to 0.23, and one run that converged read 0.216). The global norm did: 99 to 114 for healthy runs against 4,085 to 12,189 for runaways. The speed per step helped as well.
deeper: It is the same idea as a hiker's track: a meandering route (low efficiency) is not necessarily bad, but a fast, huge, lockstep move of every layer (high speed, huge norm) was the runaway signature in our DoRA runs.

quiz.q: What does path efficiency measure?
options: Straight-line distance moved divided by the length of the route
quiz.why: A value of 1 would be a perfectly straight route.

quiz.q: Did path efficiency alone tell healthy and runaway DoRA runs apart?
options: No, a converged run read 0.216, inside the runaways' 0.14 to 0.23
quiz.why: The ranges overlapped, so it needed the global norm.

quiz.q: Which measurement separated the healthy runs from the runaways in our DoRA runs?
options: The global norm (99 to 114 against thousands)
quiz.why: The runaways' global norm was thousands against about a hundred for healthy runs.

plain: A run has converged when it stops improving in the way you care about; in generative audio the loss alone is a poor way to tell.
ours: In latent-diffusion fine-tuning the loss often changes little while the model keeps getting better or worse to the ear. About half of the held-out loss sits at high noise levels and barely depends on the optimizer. On the larger set every curve was still falling at 10 epochs, and the setting that finished best led only from epoch 8 of 10, so short runs rank learning speed, not final quality. We choose checkpoints by listening.
deeper: Convergence by the loss curve means the curve is flat; convergence to a good result needs a check that fits your data, and the guide adds stop rules (a non-finite loss, the held-out loss rising for several epochs) to end clearly bad runs early. We cannot prove a run has converged from the loss alone.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a run to have converged?
options: It has stopped improving in the way you care about
quiz.why: Reaching the end of the schedule does not mean convergence.

quiz.q: Why is a flat loss a weak proof of convergence in latent diffusion?
options: A large part of the loss sits at noise levels the model cannot change
quiz.why: Much of the loss is irreducible, so audible progress shows up as a small change.

quiz.q: In one sweep the best setting led only from epoch 8 of 10. What does that say about short runs?
options: They rank learning speed, not final quality
quiz.why: Early rankings may reverse later.

plain: Fine-tuning continues training a model that is already trained, on a smaller set of data, to bend it toward a particular style or task.
ours: Our fine-tunes of Stable Audio 3 are of two kinds: full fine-tunes, which change every weight of the model (a few runs, several failures), and LoRA or DoRA adapters, which train a small add-on while the original weights stay fixed. Full fine-tunes need a lot of memory. In a memory test (GHOST-NOTE journal, 2026-09-07), LionSR, a bf16 Lion with stochastic rounding, fits a full fine-tune of Medium Base on a 16 GB card where AdamW runs out of memory at 15.13 GiB. We have not trained a Lion full fine-tune to completion; every Lion run that trained was an adapter.
deeper: Two papers report that Muon brings no clear advantage over AdamW for full fine-tuning of Adam-pretrained models, and that LoRA reduces the gap. Switching to a different optimizer than the one used in pre-training also makes a fine-tune more sensitive to the learning rate and causes more forgetting.

quiz.q: What is fine-tuning?
options: Continuing to train an already trained model on new data
quiz.why: It starts from a trained model.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a full fine-tune and a LoRA?
options: A full fine-tune changes every weight; a LoRA trains a small add-on
A full fine-tune uses less memory
quiz.why: LoRA keeps the original weights fixed and learns a small correction.

quiz.q: Switching the optimizer relative to pre-training does what, according to the paper the guide cites?
options: Makes fine-tuning more sensitive to the learning rate and causes more forgetting
Removes the need for a learning rate
quiz.why: That is one of the paper's findings.

plain: Pre-training is the first, large training that gives a model its general ability, before any fine-tuning on a specific style or task.
ours: Which optimizer pre-trained Stable Audio 3 is not stated in its report. The report says the post-training stage used Muon at a learning rate of 1e-5 on the attention and feed-forward matrices and AdamW at 1e-6 on the rest. A developer's unpublished remark, noted in our logs, is that Muon became available late in the project, so the base model is probably mostly AdamW-shaped; treat that as a pointer, not as a published fact.
deeper: It matters because the optimizer that shaped the weights seems to matter for how well another optimizer can fine-tune them (the fine-tuning paper). Do not copy a learning rate from a from-scratch setup to a fine-tune.

quiz.q: What is pre-training?
options: The first large training that gives general ability
quiz.why: Fine-tuning builds on it.

quiz.q: Does the Stable Audio 3 report state which optimizer pre-trained it?
quiz.why: The guide notes that the report is silent on this.

quiz.q: How should the developer's remark about Muon arriving late be treated?
options: As an unpublished pointer, not a published fact
quiz.why: The guide labels it a pointer from our notes.

plain: A diffusion model generates by starting from noise and removing it step by step until a clean result remains, guided by what it learned during training.
ours: Stable Audio 3 is a rectified-flow diffusion model: during training an example is mixed with noise by a randomly chosen amount t (0 for clean, 1 for pure noise) and the model learns to predict how to undo it. Our control heads are trained on the same kind of noisy latents at random noise levels, so the loss has a share at every noise level.
deeper: That is why the held-out loss is split by noise level t: the same model is asked to do very different jobs at t near 0 (refine detail) and t near 1 (decide the layout). It also means the time (noise level) is an input to the network, which the time-embedding layers handle.

quiz.q: How does a diffusion model generate?
options: By removing noise from random noise step by step
quiz.why: Generation is a gradual denoising.

quiz.q: In rectified flow, what does t = 1 mean?
quiz.why: t runs from 0 (clean) to 1 (pure noise).

quiz.q: Why is the held-out loss split by noise level?
options: The model does very different jobs at different noise levels
Because t is the batch size
It is required by the GPU
quiz.why: Detail refinement at low t and layout at high t behave differently.

plain: A latent is a compressed internal representation of the audio: a grid of numbers much smaller than the waveform, which the model works on and a decoder turns back into sound.
ours: Our models work on SAME latents: 256 channels, with one time step for every 4,096 audio samples (about 10.8 per second). The guide uses the standard deviation of generated latents as a health check: about 1.1 is healthy, and values from 1.3 up were the early stage of the drone.
deeper: The latent is trained to carry musical information in a form that is nearly linear to read out (chroma and text are close to one linear map away). A decoder trained to tolerate small noise turns the latent back into audio, which is why steering and mixing in latent space decode cleanly.

quiz.q: What is a latent?
options: A compressed internal representation of the audio
quiz.why: The model works on latents, not on raw waveforms.

quiz.q: How many channels does a SAME latent have?
quiz.why: 256 channels, at about 10.8 time steps per second.

quiz.q: What did a latent standard deviation of 1.3 or more indicate in the guide?
options: The early stage of the drone from weight growth
quiz.why: Healthy is near 1.1; larger values warned of runaway growth.
